summary: MPL has a set of parameters that normally should be identical for every forwarder in a network. This standards-track RFC defines a DHCPv6 option for distributing the MPL parameter set so that it can be configured in one place instead of on each device.

eli5.summary: Instead of telling every kid the game rules one by one, you post them once on the wall for everyone to read.

questions: what is the mpl dhcpv6 option
subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that hands every low-power mesh node the same multicast tuning settings from one place.

tldr.problem: MPL has 10 parameters that should be the same on every forwarder in an MPL Domain, but RFC 7731 defines no way to configure them across a network.
tldr.mechanism: The new DHCPv6 option OPTION_MPL_PARAMETERS (code 104) carries the whole parameter set, either for one named MPL Domain or as a wildcard default for all domains.
tldr.outcome: A managed network can configure its MPL forwarders from the DHCPv6 server, and forwarders suspend themselves if they lose contact with it.

today: RFC 7774 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of how DHCPv6 distributes MPL parameters.

sections.title: Why MPL Needs Configuring
sections.content:
The Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL, RFC 7731) spreads multicast messages across networks such as wireless meshes. Its parameters control the trade-off between end-to-end delay and network utilization. In most environments the defaults are acceptable, but some environments need careful tuning.

Section 5.4 of RFC 7731 says each parameter should be the same for all nodes in an MPL Domain, yet RFC 7731 defines no way to configure them. Managed wireless mesh networks often already run a DHCP server, so this RFC distributes the parameter sets through a new DHCPv6 option.
sections.eli5: A group of tiny devices all need to follow the same rules for passing messages along. This RFC gives the network boss one easy way to hand out those rules.

sections.title: The Ten MPL Parameters and Domains
sections.content:
An MPL Domain is identified by an MPL Domain Address, an IPv6 multicast address. Each domain has 10 parameters: PROACTIVE_FORWARDING, SEED_SET_ENTRY_LIFETIME, and four each for data messages and control messages (_IMIN, _IMAX, _K and _TIMER_EXPIRATIONS).

One network may have several domains with different settings. To configure more than one, a DHCP server may give a client more than one MPL Parameter Configuration Option.
sections.eli5: Each group of devices has ten dials. Different groups in the same network can have their dials set differently, so the server can send one note per group.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The option is OPTION_MPL_PARAMETERS, DHCPv6 option code 104. The option_len field MUST be 16 if no MPL Domain Address is present, or 32 if one is (a 128-bit address follows the parameters).

The first bit, P, is set when PROACTIVE_FORWARDING is TRUE. The next 7 bits (Z) are reserved: servers MUST set them to zero and clients SHOULD ignore them. TUNIT is the unit of time for the timer parameters, in milliseconds.

Timer values are stored divided by TUNIT. For example, if TUNIT is 20 and the minimum data message interval is 1000 ms, DM_IMIN is set to 50. The *_IMAX values are numbers of doublings of the minimum interval, as in the Trickle algorithm (RFC 6206). With TUNIT 10, C_IMIN 50 and C_IMAX 6, the maximum interval is 32 seconds (500 ms * 2^6).

Zero and all-ones values are reserved in the timer and count fields and MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: The note is a small form with boxes for each dial setting. Times are written in chunks of a chosen size, so a short number can stand for a long wait.

sections.title: Client, Forwarder, Server and Relay Behavior
sections.content:
A client MAY request the option through the Option Request Option and MUST support receiving several of them. A node that receives it SHOULD join the MPL Domain and act as an MPL Forwarder with the given parameters, though local resource limits may stop it.

Priority from high to low is: the specific configuration for the domain (option_len 32), the wildcard configuration (option_len 16), then the defaults in RFC 7731. There MUST be at most one option per domain or wildcard, so option order does not matter. A node MUST leave a domain that is missing from an updated, all-valid set, unless it has a manual configuration for it.

If a client cannot get a valid response within T2 (stateful) or twice the information refresh time (stateless), it MUST suspend the forwarders configured by this option, but not those configured by other means. Clients MUST ignore all MPL options in a message if any contains an invalid value, and the message is then treated as not received for MPL purposes.

Servers send the option only if configured with values and the client requested it, and MUST ignore an incoming copy. Relays have no additional requirements.
sections.eli5: Devices ask the server for the rules and follow them. If the server goes quiet for too long, they stop passing messages along rather than follow stale rules.

sections.title: Updating Parameters
sections.content:
Updates are not synchronized, so nodes may briefly hold different parameter sets. RFC 6206 describes problems that occur when Trickle timers do not match between neighbors. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS not updating a domain's parameters too often, with about once per information refresh time interval (such as T1) as a reasonable rate.

Inconsistent sets may reduce performance but still work if both old and new sets suit the communication load. Operators need to know which nodes have not yet updated. Where updates are very infrequent, Reconfigure messages may keep forwarders in sync.
sections.eli5: If you change the rules often, some kids will still be playing by the old ones. So change them rarely, and make sure both versions still work.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
IANA assigned option code 104 for OPTION_MPL_PARAMETERS in the DHCPv6 Option Codes registry.

A forged parameter set may cause excessive Layer 2 broadcasting, so implementations should set reasonable bounds, for example not setting K too high or IMIN too low. The DHCP server or network should be trusted, for example through DHCPv6 authentication, though constrained networks may not support it. In that case other integrity methods should be applied, and DHCPv6 packets SHOULD be filtered at the border router, except for traffic with a remote DHCPv6 server or relays that manage the network.
sections.eli5: A prankster who sends fake rules could make every device shout at once. So devices should only trust the real server and refuse silly settings.
